title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
setting: online experiment with short story writers
ai_method: large language model (LLM) providing story ideas
comparison: writers with AI-generated ideas vs writers without AI assistance
outcomes: individual creativity (story creativity ratings), writing quality, enjoyment, collective diversity of novel content (story similarity)
key_findings: Access to generative AI ideas increased story creativity, writing quality, and enjoyment, especially for less creative writers, but made stories more similar to each other, reducing collective novelty.

title: Creativity from Friction: Human-AI Interaction for Exploratory Structural Design
sample_or_dataset: 3 expert participants (architecture, structural engineering, parametric modelling)
ai_method: Google Gemini 3.1 Flash‑Lite (generative AI reasoning model) integrated in a multimodal design interface
comparison: no explicit control condition; participants used the AI‑supported interface and reflected on its impact versus their usual workflow
outcomes: perceived reduction of repetitive modelling friction, generation of new design ideas (e.g., circular internal court), design revisions prompted by AI interaction, participants’ categorisation of interaction as automation, collaboration, or co‑creation
key_findings: All three experts reported that the AI‑supported process reduced unproductive modelling friction and enabled novel design concepts, such as a circular internal court, with participants revising their designs multiple times. Participants described the interaction variably as automation, collaboration, or co‑creation, indicating the AI acted as a supportive co‑creative partner. The study suggests a positive effect of generative AI on creative exploration in structural design.
limitations: very small sample (n=3), prototype interface lacking full CAD functionality, limited AI autonomy (design changes mainly initiated by designers), no causal evidence that AI alone caused higher creativity.

title: How Creatives Approach GenAI Image Generation: Tensions Between Structured Guidance, Self-Experimentation, and Creative Autonomy
setting: lab‑based sessions with participants recruited from university and online communities
sample_or_dataset: 17 participants (6F/10M/1 gender‑non‑conforming) from various creative professions
outcomes: confusion (5‑point Likert), satisfaction (5‑point Likert), confidence (5‑point Likert), enjoyment (5‑point Likert)
key_findings: When using structured guidance, participants reported slightly lower confusion (M=2.33 vs 2.68) and higher satisfaction (M=3.91 vs 3.36) compared with self‑experimentation; confidence and enjoyment were comparable across conditions.
limitations: small sample size (n=17), potential self‑selection bias in survey respondents, limited measurement of technical expertise, and findings may not generalize beyond early‑stage ideation tasks.

title: Generative AI in Game Design: Enhancing Creativity or Constraining Innovation?
ai_method: generative AI tools used in game design
outcomes: ideation speed, prototyping efficiency, automation of repetitive tasks, originality concerns, creative dependency, human-authored content integrity
key_findings: Generative AI accelerated ideation, enhanced prototyping, and automated repetitive tasks, but raised concerns about originality, creative dependency, and the undermining of human-authored content.

title: Telling Creative Stories Using Generative Visual Aids
setting: online creative writing task using a web interface, participants recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk
sample_or_dataset: adult participants fluent in English; 362 stories analyzed (exact participant count not reported)
ai_method: generative visual algorithms (BigGAN, VQGAN, DALL‑E, CLIPDraw) combined with CLIP
comparison: visual aid condition (V+) vs control condition with no visuals (V‑)
outcomes: creativity, originality, level of completion, visualizability, plot quality, integration of starting prompt, fun rating, story length (characters)
key_findings: Writers who could view AI‑generated visuals produced stories rated higher on creativity, originality, completion, visualizability and plot (p<0.05) and reported the task as more fun (4.126 ± 0.908 vs 4.307 ± 0.808, p=0.0453); their stories were longer (828 vs 796 characters). However, the control group integrated the original prompt better (p<0.05).

title: Ai.llude: Encouraging Rewriting AI-Generated Text to Support Creative Expression
setting: creative writing task (short story) using a web-based AI writing assistant
ai_method: generative AI writing assistant providing fluent continuations and intermediate suggestions designed to encourage rewriting
outcomes: percentage of AI‑generated text retained in final story, sentence embedding similarity between suggestion and final text, number of text‑insert and text‑delete operations, self‑reported need to rewrite, motivation to read/evaluate suggestions
key_findings: Writers kept significantly less of intermediate suggestions (16% of text) than fluent continuations (60%) and showed lower semantic similarity (0.28 vs 0.63). They performed nearly double the number of edits for intermediate suggestions (795 vs 444) and reported a higher need to rewrite them (p=0.025). Intermediate suggestions thus promoted more active rewriting and reflection.
limitations: Sample limited to young, mostly college‑aged writers with similar geographic background; fixed list of intermediate prompts may not generalize; participants perceived intermediate suggestions as lower quality, which could affect motivation; study did not measure longer‑term creativity outcomes.

title: Dialogue with the Machine and Dialogue with the Art World: Evaluating Generative AI for Culturally-Situated Creativity
setting: artistic practice within Persian Gulf cultural context (art worlds)
sample_or_dataset: 3 artists and 3 expert commentators (participants recruited via snowball sampling)
ai_method: generative image models (e.g., MidJourney, DALL‑E, Adobe Firefly, Stable Diffusion, Google Colab)
comparison: none (within‑subject exploration of tool use before and after dialogue workshops)
outcomes: creative process adaptation, cultural representation in generated artwork, identification of tool limitations (e.g., text generation), development of decentralized culturally‑situated datasets
key_findings: Dialogues with commentators and the machine enabled artists to shift their use of generative AI tools toward culturally relevant representations, leading to the creation of decentralized datasets and novel artistic outputs, while also highlighting limitations such as poor text generation. Participants reported enhanced creative agency and awareness of socio‑technical dynamics.
limitations: very small sample (3 artists, 3 commentators), qualitative only, no quantitative comparison or control condition, findings may not generalize beyond the specific cultural context.

title: Evaluating Beyond the Screen: Collective Assessment of AI-Generated Business Plans with Resource-Constrained Entrepreneurs
setting: Community entrepreneurship workshops in Maryland, USA
sample_or_dataset: Workshop attendees (N=14) who used the BizChat AI‑powered business‑planning tool
ai_method: BizChat – an AI‑generated business‑plan generator with an evaluation module linking claims to user input
comparison: Collective (think‑pair‑share) evaluation vs. typical solo, on‑screen evaluation
outcomes: Use of printed copies and rubrics, Peer‑based verification of AI‑generated claims, Extended evaluation beyond the workshop (sharing printed plans), Perceived reduction of verification burden
key_findings: Participants reported that linking AI‑generated claims to their original inputs and conducting evaluation in a group setting enabled concrete, personal assessments; they printed plans, applied shared rubrics, and sought peer feedback, suggesting that collective evaluation scaffolds understanding of AI output.
limitations: Very small sample (n=14), early‑stage and exploratory with no quantitative measures of creativity or entrepreneurial competency, limited generalizability.

title: Generative AI in international hotel marketing: impacts on employee creativity and performance
ai_method: generative AI tools integrated into marketing workflows
key_findings: Technological competence, organizational support and government support significantly influence AI-driven innovative behavior, which in turn enhances employee creativity and performance; creativity mediates the relationship between innovative behavior and performance.

title: Do AI-generative tools kill or nurture creativity in EFL teaching and learning?
Harmony or Discord? The Intersection of Generative AI and Human Creativity in Advertising
ai_method: generative AI tools for advertising creative work
comparison: none (exploratory study of AI vs. human creativity)
outcomes: human creativity, entrepreneurial competencies (brand strategy, emotional connection), ethical considerations, risk of creative homogenization
key_findings: Generative AI reshapes creativity by handling routine tasks, allowing human insights to focus on brand strategy and emotional connections; however, concerns arise about creative homogenization and ethical implications, indicating a mixed impact.
limitations: Sample size and quantitative measures not reported; findings based on self‑reported interviews.

title: An exploration of the role of generative AI in fostering creativity in architectural learning environments
setting: architectural learning environment (student-led AI drawing competition)
ai_method: generative AI tool for image generation (text‑to‑image)
outcomes: creativity of text prompts, creativity of AI‑generated images, perceived support for creativity (Creativity Support Index), student sentiment
key_findings: Semantic analysis showed varied conceptual richness in prompts, with higher divergence linked to more expressive images. CSI scores indicated strong support for exploratory and goal‑directed creativity, and sentiment analysis revealed strong student engagement with the AI tool.
limitations: No control or comparison condition; sample size not reported; focus limited to creativity without measuring entrepreneurial outcomes.

title: IS AI TRUST A BARRIER OR A BOOSTER? A POSTERIORI SEGMENTATION OF GENERATIVE AI ENTREPRENEURSHIP INTENTION AMONG INDONESIAN YOUTH
setting: Indonesia (Indonesian youth who have used ChatGPT)
comparison: trust in AI vs no trust (direct effect) and indirect effect via AI skills
key_findings: AI trust does not have a significant direct association with digital entrepreneurship intention, but it positively relates to AI skills and indirectly increases intention through capability development; segmentation shows heterogeneous subgroups.
